title: See, thy fleece is drenched
html_source:
In the book of Judges in the Bible, Gideon is called upon to lead a relatively small force of Israelites against a massive army of Middianites. Gideon wanted to make sure God was with him, so he proposed a test; “Behold, I will put a fleece of wool in the floor; and if the dew be on the fleece only, and it be dry upon the earth beside, this shall I know that thou wilt save Israel by my hand, as thou has said.” As indicated here, on the morrow the fleece was not just wet, it was drenched, and so Gideon was able to successfully lead a group that was whittled down to 300 men against the opposing army of 130,000, suggesting God’s abundant favor.

This entire passage honors Theodore Purefoy, and extols his virtues, having sired the newly born infant. Of course, the father’s role here is minimal, given without any thought of creating a new person. But, at least he is married, and he is not doing anything to prevent conception as he engages with his wife. This is high satire, in that it is the wife who faces the ordeal of nine months of pregnancy and the painful process of labor and delivery. As we have seen before, the references in the chapter, as throughout Ulysses, deal with the process of literary creation. Joyce implies, once again, that fatherhood is not as true a trope for that process as is motherhood, and that the course of creating superior literary art takes time and great and often painful effort.
